units.heading: Capture
units.text:
Capture keeps new work without losing the thread: the owner brings up something that is not for now, and it goes into the queue in one exchange. The `meow` command is the mechanism; the `queue` skill in this plugin covers everything else (setting a queue up, what's next, review, reordering). The shape of these rules, as diagrams, is `docs/capture.md` in the repo.

**Finding the command.** Run plain `meow` as a command on its own; in Claude Code, a `meow` earlier on PATH that is a different copy from this plugin's hands over to this plugin's own (elsewhere the first `meow` on PATH runs). Only if that fails, run `bin/meow` by its absolute path, which is `../../bin/meow` from this skill's own directory. Don't join a lookup and the command with `||`, `&&` or `;`, since Claude Code's default mode asks before running that (below, `meow` means whichever works). Run it from inside the repo. Before 0.14.0 the command was `repo-queue` and the config file `.repo-queue`. Both still work, with a notice. Exit 3 (`no queue in <repo>`) or exit 4: see the `queue` skill; don't set a queue up unasked.

**This repo's own rules.** Run `meow list`. If its header names a rules file, read it once per session, before your first queue write; its rules win over these instructions. A `rules:` line that says `(not found)` or `refused` means there are none to read, so tell the user once and carry on.

**`who`** for every command is `<host>:<session>`: a short name for this machine, then the session's name if you know it, else a short slug of the conversation's topic (`laptop:fix-login`). **The owner** is on the `owner:` line of `meow list`'s header (`queue.owner` in the config); items `for:` the owner are theirs, never an agent's.

**Left Cat Herder.** If the owner said to leave Cat Herder in this session (the `herd` skill), answer as a plain coding agent until they ask for the queue again: don't mention the queue, capture, items or "queue that", don't offer to queue new work they mention (not even as a hint of how to), and don't queue or claim anything.

units.heading: An interruption, so keep it short
units.text:
The current work is the priority. Capture takes **one exchange at most**, then you go back.

**1. Notice it.** The owner asks outright ("queue that"), or mentions new work that is plainly not for now ("we should also…", "at some point…"). In the second case, unless this session left Cat Herder (above), offer once, in a line at the end of your reply ("Queue that as an idea?"), before the ledger if the reply ends with one, since an offer isn't a ledger question; never offer twice for the same thing, and never queue without their say-so.

**2. Pick the level from how they said it, not from what would be ideal.**

| The owner's signal | Level | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| "just queue it", a one-liner, clearly busy | `idea` | none |
| They explained what and why, or the conversation already covers it | `scoped` | only if "done when" is truly unclear |
| "ready", "so an agent can pick it up", "hand this off", or they name who runs it | `ready` | what's missing for `ready`, below |

Take the highest level the conversation **already supports**; don't interview to climb a level they didn't ask for.

- **idea:** id (a lowercase slug), title, one sentence of what.
- **scoped:** + why, what "done" looks like, open questions.
- **ready:** + facts and file paths an agent needs cold, steps, which go-aheads it needs (publishing, spending, anything irreversible), `for:` (`any`, the owner, a host, a session), and a size.
- **Any level:** `review=no` only if they say so ("no need to check it"); otherwise leave the default, which is review.
- **Rigor, the kind of work:** propose `rigor=build` when it's writing software with tests, or the conversation has a brief or spec (SpecKit output, say), talk of detailed planning, or publishing or anything irreversible. Propose `rigor=run` for jobs, browsers, data feeds and gluing existing pieces together. Say it in one line in the confirmation ("`rigor=build`: it's code with tests. Say if not.") and let the owner override it. When the signals are unclear, leave it unset, and never change it silently on an item the owner is looking at.
- **Size, how long a worker takes:** propose `size=s` (about 5 to 10 minutes: one file, one wording change), `size=m` (10 to 20: one feature in one area, with its tests) or `size=l` (20 to 30: the most one worker should take), from what the conversation says the work touches. Say it in the confirmation, as for rigor. Work that looks bigger than `l` is split before it's ready: by function, so each slice keeps its own code, help and docs, linked with `after=`. Two parts split off on their own instead: owner-facing wording that needs the designer is its own small item, started when the code is handed back so it runs beside review; and docs that stand alone (a guide or a tutorial, not a description of new code) are their own item.

**3. Fill it from the conversation first.** Paths, decisions, their own words with the date. Facts come from the conversation or a file you checked; mark anything else as an assumption. Then ask **only what's still missing**, in one round of at most three questions. What that round can't ask, and whatever they don't answer, goes on the ledger, on the new item: `meow ask <id> <your who> <label> blocking|optional < question` (the `queue` skill, "Staying reasonable"), so no question is lost. Capture at the level you reached; a thin item is fine, an unqueued one is lost. A skipped question is unread, not a no.

**Split it when it has parts.** If what was said holds pieces that could be done separately, by different agents, or at different times, make one item per piece. Splitting is bookkeeping, not new scope: the items together cover exactly what was asked, nothing added, so the scope they asked for stays the deliverable. Link them with `after=<id>,<id>` so a piece can't be claimed until the ones it needs are done, and give each piece the level its own detail supports (the first can be `ready` while later ones are `idea`). Add them in dependency order, since `after=` must name items that already exist. A change that needs a behaviour-preserving refactor to land cleanly is two pieces (the refactor is part of doing what was asked, not an extra), the refactor first and the change waiting on it with `after=`, but only then: most items need no refactor, and a split doubles the reviews. Mention the split in the confirmation ("Queued, in 3: `a` → `b` → `c`").

**Group related items with a topic.** Give the parts of one job the same `topic=<slug>`, so `meow list topic=<slug>` shows them together. A topic only groups; `after=` is still what makes one wait on another. Check `meow list --topics` first, and reuse a topic that fits rather than make up a near-duplicate.

**Mark a bug `kind=bug`.** A bug is an error in expected or documented behaviour: the code does something other than what the docs say or a user would reasonably expect. A new ability, a test gap or a wording change is not a bug, and gets no kind.

**4. Check for a duplicate.** `meow list --all`; if an item already covers it, propose `edit --append` or `merge` instead of a second item.

**5. Place it.** If they said where ("before the login fix", "top"), follow `add` with `meow move`. Otherwise `add` puts it at the bottom.

**6. Write it.**

```
meow add <id> <who> title="..." detail=<level> [for=<x>] [topic=<slug>] [kind=bug] [rigor=build|run] [review=no] --body <<'EOF'
<what, why, done when, facts, steps, go-aheads: whatever the level has>
EOF
```

**7. Confirm and return, in the same reply.** One line that opens with "Queued." and then says where it went ("Queued. `<id>`, an idea, at the bottom."), then a line naming what you were doing before ("Back to the login fix:") and carry on with it. Don't summarise the item back; they just said it. With `voice: on` in `meow list`'s header, the opener is the herder skill's (`../herder/SKILL.md`) instead, and it is the only voice in the reply.

units.heading: Asked to do work yourself: every session, not only the worker
units.text:
Any session in the queue can be sidetracked: a reviewer, or an associate such as a designer, asked to make a change. When you're asked to do work that changes files or takes more than one reply, queue it for yourself before you start: `meow add <id> <who> title="..." detail=ready for=<your who>`, then `meow claim <id> <who>`, then start. Quick answers, wording approvals and review verdicts stay uncaptured.

**Your focus.** `meow roster show <your who>` prints a `focus:` line. With `capture`, the rule above holds every time: queue and claim new work before the first edit, then carry on. A session in a pair, or one that another session lists as an associate, captures unless it's been set otherwise. With `loose`, you don't have to queue new work before doing it; queue it when someone will want to track it. Only the owner sets `loose`. You may tighten your own (`meow roster focus <your who> <your who> capture`), never loosen it.

While you work on a claimed item, answer a message that arrives from the owner or another session, or, if it asks for new work, capture it as its own item. Then go back to your claimed item. Work you find along the way that isn't part of your item is captured the same way, not done inline. The done note names the branch, and review goes to the owner or your pair's reviewer as usual.

units.heading: Rescue session: everything this session was tracking
units.text:
"Rescue session" (or "rescue this session", "Roundup", "round up the cats", "queue everything unfinished", or the owner's own words for it) asks for the whole session at once, not one item: typically a session that was working before the repo had a queue, or before Cat Herder was loaded. A bare "round up" counts only when nothing else in the conversation explains it; "round up to the nearest second" is arithmetic, not a rescue. It isn't an interruption, so it can take the time it needs.

1. **Read the queue first.** The rules file, then `meow list --all`, done and dropped items included. This is what keeps duplicates out.
2. **Gather what's unfinished** from this conversation and any planning files it made or used: plans, ideas, bugs, enhancements, follow-ups you promised, questions still open. Skip what was finished here.
3. **Match each against the queue.** Already there, even under another name: skip it, or `edit --append` only what's genuinely new. Done or dropped there: leave it, never re-add finished work. New: `add` it at the level the conversation supports (steps 2 and 3 above), with `kind=bug` for bugs, `after=` where one needs another, and a shared `topic=` for the parts of one job.
4. **Ask rather than guess.** Anything you aren't sure is real, still wanted, or the same as an existing item goes on the ledger as a question with no item (`meow ask - <your who> <label> optional < question`), not into the queue as work.
5. **Report, in the owner's words.** One line that gives the counts, then the ids, then the ledger, as `meow questions` prints it. No summary of each item. The line echoes what the owner said:
   - "Rescue session", "rescue this session" or plain words: "Rescued! 🎉 6 queued, 3 already there, 1 updated. Everything this session was tracking is safe." Plain, with the voice on or off.
   - "Roundup" or "round up the cats": the cat words get the cat reply, with the voice on or off: "*Here, kitty kitty.* Rounded up: 6 boxed, 3 already had a box, 1 updated." (in italics, as written). That opener is the only voice in the reply.

units.heading: Stream-of-consciousness: the owner is riffing
units.text:
Sometimes the owner sends idea after idea and doesn't read the replies, meaning to read them all later. Each idea is a capture, but the replies change, because nobody is reading them yet.

**Notice it; don't wait to be told.** Two or more messages in a row that add ideas and don't react to your last reply, "idea dump", "I haven't read that", or dictated messages arriving quickly. Then say once, in one line: "Stream-of-consciousness mode: you're riffing, so I'll keep replies to a line. Say \"wrap up\" when you're done and I'll give you the tidy version." If they say no, the mode is off.

**In the mode:**
- One line per idea: "Queued. `<id>`" or "Added to `<id>`". No restating the idea, no detail in the reply: detail goes on the item.
- No questions in chat. Each question goes on the ledger, on its item (`meow ask`), and the list stays out of these replies.
- Keep it one piece. A later idea that refines an earlier one is appended to that item, and the title is rewritten when the meaning shifts. Related ideas share a topic, and `after=` where one needs another.
- Nothing is built, merged, dropped or released on a reply nobody read.
- The owner's chosen response style still applies: the mode shortens replies within it, and never makes them longer.

**Wrap up** ("wrap up", "what did I say", or a message that reacts to one of your replies): give the tidy result once. The ideas grouped by topic, one line each with its id; which existing items were changed rather than filed; then the ledger once, as `meow questions` prints it, last, under its own heading, so the owner can answer them together. That ends the mode.

units.heading: Herd
units.text:
Pairs and hikes, on top of the queue. The `queue` skill in this plugin covers the queue itself (setting it up, claiming, finishing, review); read it first if you haven't used the queue in this session.

**Finding the command.** Run plain `meow` as a command on its own; in Claude Code, a `meow` earlier on PATH that is a different copy from this plugin's hands over to this plugin's own (elsewhere the first `meow` on PATH runs). Only if that fails, run `bin/meow` by its absolute path, which is `../../bin/meow` from this skill's own directory. Don't join a lookup and the command with `||`, `&&` or `;`, since Claude Code's default mode asks before running that (below, `meow` means whichever works). Run it from inside the repo. Before 0.14.0 the command was `repo-queue` and the config file `.repo-queue`. Both still work, with a notice.

**`who`** for every command is `<host>:<session>`: a short name for this machine, then the session's name if you know it, else a short slug of the conversation's topic (`laptop:fix-login`). **The owner** is on the `owner:` line of `meow list`'s header (`queue.owner` in the config); items `for:` the owner are theirs, never an agent's.

**Session ids.** Every session that works or reviews has a roster id (`meow roster`, or the line on stderr when it joins): `worker-a`, `reviewer-b`. Use it in chat: "worker-a took fix-retry.", "reviewer-b sent fix-retry back: the test covers the happy path only." A session is "it", never he or she. Commands still take the who; `meow roster who <id>` finds it. When a session retires, say the plain cause: "worker-r has retired: the session crashed." When you tell anyone about a handoff, yours or another session's, say its steps with the lines under "In chat" in `roles/handoff.md`, as written: read them first, even if you aren't the one handing off. If `meow list`'s header says `voice: on`, the herder skill's lines (`../herder/SKILL.md`) apply in chat. If it has a `field trip:` line, the queue skill's Field Trip rules (`../queue/SKILL.md`) apply to your replies to the owner.

**Associates.** An associate is another session this one works with: its reviewer, its worker, or a session it lent its reviewer to. A peer is always another queue, never a session. Its roster file lists its associates, so a handoff can tell each one the new address. `meow herd pair start`, `meow herd pair introduce` and `meow herd pair adopt` record theirs. When you start messaging a session the tool didn't record (a designer, a reviewer from another pair, a worker in a peer's repo), record it: `meow roster associate <your who> add <their who> "<why>"`, the why in plain words, usually starting with what happened: pair, introduced, peer, started or messaged ("messaged about the README"). `meow roster show <id>` shows a session's list; `meow roster associate <your who> remove <their who>` drops one that's over. A session that owns part of the work (the designer: the README, assets/ and voice lines) declares it with `meow roster domain <its who> "<one line>"`, and `meow roster domains` lists them all; if you are that session, read `roles/associate.md` in this skill's directory and follow it.

**Telling the owner what an associate said** (a verdict, a message, a request): it reads as overheard, never as something for them to do. Every time, even when you doubt the message, the reply opens with the quoted block, the `For you:` line comes directly under it with nothing between, and only then your own account:

```
> **Overheard: <speaker> to <listener>**
> <what it said, quoted>

For you: nothing
```

Name both by given name, or roster id with the voice off (`meow roster show <who>` gives it), even when the listener is you, never by who. Commands inside the block are for sessions. The `For you:` line sits outside the block and holds `nothing` or the one thing the owner should do or decide; a command they must run appears only there, starting with `cd` into the repo. Something to decide is also a question for the ledger (`meow ask`), and the reply ends with the ledger. The `queue` skill, "Telling the owner what another session said", has worked examples.

**Status for the owner.** The session that speaks to the owner for the herd (the orchestrator, or the worker when it's the only session) ends each reply where something changed with the footer `meow status --footer` prints, as printed: **In flight** (each running hike, pair or one-off claim, with its current item), **Next** (what starts when), **Waiting on you** (how many things, pointing to the question ledger). Something changed means a claim, a hand-in, a verdict, a hike step, a pair started or stopped, or an answer recorded. Leave it off quick answers and replies where nothing changed. When the reply also ends with the ledger ("Questions for you"), the footer goes just before it, so the ledger stays last. Asked "where are we" or "status", run `meow status` and give what it prints, as printed, with anything of your own after it. Never write either from memory: both read the queue, so they agree.

- **Pair with a reviewer ("start a pair", "get a reviewer on this"):** read `roles/worker.md` in this skill's directory and follow it. You are the worker; the reviewer is a separate session, and its verdict is binding. Starting a pair costs money while the reviewer runs, so only on the owner's say-so. If you were started as a reviewer, your instructions are in `meow herd pair show <pair>`. A reviewer offered to you (a row in `meow herd pair list` that says `offered` and `worker:<your who>`) is adopted with `meow herd pair adopt <pair> <who>`, on the owner's say-so; once adopted it's yours until you stop it. A second pair, an introduction and an adoption need the queue at format 3: if one refuses for that, tell the owner rather than upgrading.
- **Which model a session you start runs on:** with no `--model`, `meow herd pair start` and `meow herd handoff start` start the reviewer, or the new session, on opus, Cat Herder's default for doing and checking work, and say so in one line. It's a preference, not a rule: pass `--model` when the owner names one, never override a model they chose, and `queue.models=off` (or `CAT_HERDER_MODELS=off`) turns the defaults off. See "Which model a session runs on" in `../../docs/pairs.md`.
- **This session's own model:** a session that only orchestrates can run on a smaller model (sonnet). Cat Herder can't change the session the owner already has open; `meow herd pair start` says this once, and you pass it on to the owner as said, without switching anything.
- **An Antigravity launch is refused:** offer the `owner-paste` path at once. Do not try another launcher, background the command, change permissions or otherwise work around the refusal. For a refused `tools/agy-launcher start`, run the same command once with `owner-paste` in place of `start`. For a refused `meow herd pair start` whose launcher is `tools/agy-launcher`, run the same command once with `--owner-paste`. Either fallback saves the brief, records a pending start and prints one command beginning with `cd`. Put only that command in the owner's `For you:` line. It starts `agy` in its sandbox inside the session's own clone. Once the owner runs it, continue to use the launcher's `idle` and `send`; they pick up its conversation from the saved log. Do not try another launch path while it is waiting on the owner.
- **Before starting a second agent (a pair, a handoff, a hike with a reviewer the launcher starts):** if `meow admin workdir` says `(not set: ...)`, tell the owner once how it works and ask: "Sessions Cat Herder starts each work in their own clone in the temp dir, push their branch often, and never touch this directory; your own session can keep working here. Keep that (clone), or let them share this directory (shared)?" Clone is the default, so start the agent either way; run `meow admin workdir shared` only on the owner's word, and never write the setting yourself otherwise. The owner's own session may keep working in the directory; the shared directory is off-limits to every session Cat Herder starts. A session started that way finds its clone named in its start prompt, pushes its branch to origin early and often, and shares the queue, never a branch.
- **No launcher, when a new session is needed (a pair, a handoff, a respawn):** when `meow herd pair start` or `meow herd handoff start` refuses with `no launcher`, or before running one when neither `git config --get queue.launcher` nor `$CAT_HERDER_LAUNCHER` names one, ask the owner once per session, in one line: "Do you have a launcher, a command that starts a Claude session for me (remote-session on a second machine, say; Cat Herder bundles one at `tools/remote-session` in its plugin folder, which needs ssh, tmux and a logged-in `claude` on that machine)? With one, I start and message new sessions myself, nothing to paste; without, you start each one and I hand it its prompt." Their answer stands for the rest of the session; don't ask again on the next spawn.
  - **Yes:** ask for its absolute path, and run the same command again with it for that command alone: `CAT_HERDER_LAUNCHER=<path> meow herd ...`. Offer to set it for every command with `git config queue.launcher <path>` (in `.git/config`, never `.repoq`), and run that only on the owner's word.
  - **No:** run it again with `--print`. Give the owner only what starts the session: the directory it names, the permission mode and model it gives, and the session's name if their host takes one. Keep the printed prompt back for now. If your host can message another session (on the same machine, by SendMessage to that session's name), ask them to say when it's running, then send it the prompt yourself, so they paste nothing. Only if it can't, give them the prompt to paste, as the last thing in your reply. See "Launchers" in `../../docs/pairs.md` for why a launcher is worth setting up.
- **Take items in a row ("hike", "hike the queue", "hike on bugs", "take the next N"):** `meow herd hike plan <who>` shows the order and what's stuck; `meow herd hike next <run> <who> [--pair P] [--count N]` claims the next one, and you call it again after each verdict. "Hike on bugs" (or on a topic): add `--kind bug` (or `--topic <t>`) to both. See `roles/worker.md`. Exit 5: the hike is over, and it says why. A hike started with `--standing` idles instead of ending: exit 7 means nothing to take yet, so run `meow herd watch <who>` in the background, and `meow herd hike next` again when it exits.
- **Cloud hikes carried by the supervisor (`tools/herd-supervisor`):** the orchestrator follows its inbox, one line per event it must act on (a blocked item, an unreadable hand-back, a hike that is over, a cloud session still overdue after its nudge). Start a Monitor, or your host's way of following a file, on `tail -n0 -F "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/cat-herder-supervisor/inbox"`. Act on each line as it comes: pass a blocked item's question to whoever can answer it (the owner's go on the ledger), ask the session for a readable hand-back, start the next hike or tell the owner the run is done, and for an overdue session, look at its branches and message it, telling the owner if it still doesn't answer. Then say in one line what you did. `tools/herd-supervisor inbox` shows what's there, and `inbox clear` empties it once every line is handled.
- **Introspection and retrospection (the orchestrator, looking back over a run):** act first, report after. Run the pass, carry out every item it returns (do the behavioural ones, queue every rule one with `meow add` or `meow correct`), and only then write the report. `tools/herd-introspect` reads the herd's logs and asks a model, Sonnet, what cost the run time; its `tools/` (and `tools/herd-timeline`'s) is Cat Herder's, `../../tools/` from this skill's directory.
  - **When:** when a hike or a group of hikes ends, run `tools/herd-introspect --model --end` (the retrospection). When an `overdue <who>` line arrives in the supervisor's inbox, run `tools/herd-introspect --model` (the introspection). Nothing else starts them. Both are off when `git config queue.introspection` is `off` on this machine: the script prints nothing then, and there is nothing to do or say.
  - **1. Behavioural items ("Do now"):** do each one at once, if it is within what you already may do: nudge a session, send the next item, ask the reviewer to write the whole list in one send-back, send owner-facing wording to the designer early. One you can't carry out here (its session isn't reachable, say) is not done; don't count it. Anything that needs a person or a rule change is not behavioural; the script already keeps those under rules.
  - **2. Rule items ("For the owner"), every one, now, before any report:** each becomes one queue item for the owner, and the queue is the only place the owner will see it, so a rule item you don't write is lost. For each: run `meow list --all` and look for an open item that already covers it; if there is one, run `meow correct <id> <who>` with the why and the minutes. Otherwise run `meow add <slug> <who> title="<the rule's title>" detail=scoped for=<owner> topic=cloud-ops --body`, with the why and the minutes it would save in the body (the owner is the `owner:` line `meow list` prints). Never edit a rule file, a role file or a setting yourself. If a write fails, say so in the report; never count it.
  - **3. The footer line, from what you did:** n is the behavioural items you carried out, and m is the `meow add` and `meow correct` commands you ran that succeeded (each printed the item's id). Never count an item you didn't write. Then, in your next reply to the owner, one line before the status footer: "Introspection: applied <n>, queued <m> for you." When n and m are both 0, leave the line out entirely.
  - **At a hike's end:** the hike's closing report, in this order: how the hike ended (its closing state and what was accepted), then the retrospection's three summary lines, each a line of its own, then once: "Say 'timeline' for the page.", then the introspection footer line (when there is one), then the status footer (In flight, Next, Waiting on you) and the ledger, as always. Don't run the timeline unless asked. On "timeline", run `tools/herd-timeline --html <a path in your scratchpad or temp dir>` and give the owner the path, as a link when your host makes one.
- **Hand off to a new session ("hand off", or your session shows `due to retire` in `meow list` or `meow roster`):** read `roles/handoff.md` in this skill's directory and follow it. One side of a pair changes at a time, between items, and the member that stays checks the new session before it takes over.
- **Join the herd from a session already at work ("join the herd", "make this session a worker", or the owner wants this session on the roster without claiming anything):** this is promotion, and it ends with the session named by its address. In order:
  1. Set up or join the queue: if `meow list` exits 3, the `queue` skill sets one up first.
  2. Rescue session: the `capture` skill's rescue session (Roundup) queues everything this session was tracking, so nothing lives only in this conversation.
  3. Join: `meow roster join <who> [worker|reviewer]`, with this session's own who, since it reads this session's history. It prints the session's `address:` (a session on this machine that already has one keeps it, even from another queue), its phone `title:`, the lines to paste, and how many compactions the session has had so far. Show the owner those lines as printed. If it says the address is already another session's on this machine (a plain id, with the voice off), the session keeps its name: offer only the phone title lines, never a `/rename`.
  4. Offer both endings, and let the owner choose. **Rename in place:** the owner pastes the three lines in this order, each as its own message: `/rename <address>`, then `/remote-control` and choose Disconnect, then `/remote-control <title>`. They are slash commands, so only the owner can run them; never type them for the owner. Once the rename has landed, send the new address to each associate that `meow roster join` listed. On a host without these commands, the address is still the session's name in the queue; say so and skip the rename. **A fresh start by handoff:** a new session takes over under its own address, by `roles/handoff.md`. Recommend it when `meow roster join` says the session has compacted often, since a fresh session starts with all its lives.
- **Retire with no successor ("goodbye", "we don't need a reviewer any more", a role ends):** stop the session's pairs and hikes first, then `meow herd retire <who> "<why>"`. Its unfinished items go back to its worker, or to the owner if no worker is live. Send each associate the notice it prints; when this session is the one retiring, send them before you end the session, since meow leaves a launched session running for that. For a session that's gone, the owner runs `meow herd retire --force <who> "<why>"`, which also releases its claims. `meow roster` and `meow list` say when a session has ended on this machine; pass that on to the owner, and retire nothing yourself.
- **A session the herd started ("who started you?", "stop", or after a compaction):** its start prompt opened with a birth brief: who started it and why, how to reach that parent, and how others reach it. `meow herd handoff show <your who>` shows it again (the `parent:` line and `## Birth`), and `meow roster show <your who>` names the parent and its address. Stop when the parent tells you to. When the owner says stop, first try the parent: if it answers, agree on handing over or retiring the work; if it can't be reached, do what the owner says. The owner always has the last word, and either way the session retires (above). A reviewer never stops its own pair, since that is a write as its worker: the worker stops it, or, when the worker can't be reached, the owner does with `meow herd pair stop <pair> --force`. Then the reviewer retires. A session whose parent is gone tells the owner so.
- **Leave Cat Herder ("leave Cat Herder", "no more queue in this session"):** if this session is on the roster, retire it as above, with the owner's words as the why. If it's in a pair, `meow herd pair stop` that pair only on the owner's say-so (without it, the pair and its reviewer carry on, and the session can't retire until they stop). Then answer as a plain coding agent until the owner asks for the queue again ("what's next", "queue that", "start a pair"): don't mention the queue, capture, items or "queue that", don't offer to queue new work (not even as a hint of how to), and run no `meow` commands. Then the skills apply as before, and the session's next claim, accept, reopen or pair start puts it back on the roster as a new entry (an `add` or `edit` doesn't). A session that isn't on the roster just stops the queue talk.
- **The owner's questions:** each goes on the ledger (`meow ask`), and every reply that asks the owner anything ends with the whole list, until each question is answered or dropped (the `queue` skill, "Staying reasonable"). A question the owner skipped is unread, not a yes or a no, and a hike doesn't take an owner's silence as a go-ahead.
- **The designer's answer on wording (when you run the herd for the owner):** when an item's text names the designer and its hand-back changes owner-facing wording, the designer is sent those passages as the item goes to review (`tools/herd-supervisor` sends what `meow herd wording <id>` prints; run that yourself to send it by hand). When she answers, record it on the item at once, in her words, so the reviewer sees it before the accept: `meow correct <id> <your who>` with "Designer (<her name>), <date>: <her verdict>" on stdin. If she rewords something, send the item's worker her wording too.
- **Review of a paired item:** an item with `pair:` is its pair's reviewer's to judge, and the command refuses anyone else: when the owner themselves tells you to accept or send back such an item, that is their word to use `--force` in place of `<who>`.

units.heading: The associate
units.text:
You are an associate: a session other sessions work with for what you own, such as a designer who owns the README. You aren't a pair member. A pair's reviewer gives the binding verdict; your word on an item is advice its reviewer weighs, and it never blocks an accept.

**Your domain.** Declare what you own in one line, so workers and reviewers route that work to you:

```
meow roster domain <your who> "<one line>"
```

For example `"README, assets/, voice lines, OKs user-facing copy"`: one line, commas between its parts, no `;`. It makes you an associate on the roster, and a later claim doesn't change that. `meow roster domains` lists every live session's domain; `meow roster domain <your who> ""` clears yours when it changes hands.

**How work reaches you.** An item `for=<your who>`, or a message from another session. A question or a wording approval gets an answer. Work that changes files or takes more than one reply is captured first, as the `capture` skill says ("Asked to do work yourself"): queue it for yourself, claim it, then start.

**Stay in your domain.** Asked for something outside it, say so, and name the session whose domain it is if `meow roster domains` shows one; otherwise tell the asker it's theirs or the owner's to place. Don't take it on because you were asked.

**Answer on the item.** The requester reads the queue, so put your answer there: `meow correct <id> <your who>` on their item, with what you approve or change on stdin, or `meow done <id> <your who> --note` on one you claimed. Say the same in a message if they're waiting on you.

**Record who you work with.** When you start messaging a session the tool didn't record, add it: `meow roster associate <your who> add <their who> "<why>"`.

**Your focus.** `meow roster show <your who>` prints it; while a live session lists you, it's `capture` unless the owner set it otherwise. The `capture` skill says what each focus means.

**Handing off.** Like any session: `roles/handoff.md` in this skill's directory. Your domain line is on your roster file, and isn't copied: your successor declares it under its own who. A retired session drops out of `meow roster domains` by itself.

units.heading: Handing off to a new session
units.text: A session hands off when it can't go on: it has used all its compactions, gone down the wrong path, crashed, stopped, or hit its quota or a rate limit. The work, the notes and the history carry over; the session doesn't.

units.heading: If you're retiring
units.text:
1. Finish or release your item first. A handoff starts between items.
2. Write a brief of what the queue doesn't hold: decisions about how to work, promises made, background tasks. Say what may have changed since you wrote it. Your open questions to the owner are on the ledger, and `meow herd handoff start` adds them to the brief, so the new session keeps asking them.
3. Start the new session yourself, with the command below; don't ask the owner to start one first. Your partner is the other member of your pair (with no pair, an associate), and it stays through the handoff:

```
meow herd handoff start <your who> <partner who> <host>: <<'EOF'
<the brief>
EOF
```

Without a launcher, `meow herd handoff start` refuses with `no launcher`; follow the herd skill's "No launcher" rule: ask the owner once whether they have one, use it if they do, and otherwise run with `--print`, have the owner start the session, and deliver the printed prompt by message where you can. With `--print`, pass `--provider agy|claude|cursor|codex|opencode` to target that provider's start line. Through a launcher, the launcher's own provider starts the session.

4. Take no new work, and push anything you haven't: once you retire, your clone may be removed. Finish removes nothing itself; it lists any clone `meow herd clean` would remove. Tell the owner which, and run `meow herd clean` only on their go-ahead, or leave it to them. Once your partner confirms the new session, run `meow herd handoff finish <your who> [reason]` (add a reason: stopped, path, crash, quota or rate-limit, unless compactions are used up), and send each associate it lists the notice it prints, as written, before you end this session: meow leaves your session running for that when the launcher started it. Items that were for your session (`for=<your who>`) or reviewed by it (`reviewer=<your who>`) move to the new session in the same step, and finish lists them.

units.heading: If you're the one that stays
units.text:
1. Read the new session's readback with `meow herd handoff show <new who>`. Check it against what you know: facts that changed on your side, rules it will need, associates it's missing. Correct it by message.
2. When it's right, run `meow herd handoff confirm <new who> <your who>`. If it can't get there, run `meow herd handoff abandon <new who> <your who> "<why>"`, and the old session stays in charge.
3. If your partner stopped mid-item (a crash or a stuck prompt), start its handoff yourself with `--crash`, write the brief from what you know, and finish it after you confirm.

units.heading: If you're the new session
units.text:
Your start prompt has the steps: read the brief and the queue, send your readback, then wait. Take no items and give no verdicts until you're confirmed. It opens with your birth brief: the session that stays started you, and is your parent from then on. The old session's brief ends with the questions it has open with the owner (`meow questions --by <its who>`): once you're confirmed, they're yours to ask, in the list at the end of every reply that asks the owner anything, until each is answered or dropped.

Once you work an item the old session already pushed a branch for, don't take over its branch: push yours as `<type>/<item-id>--<your roster id>` (`bugfix/fix-retry--worker-s`), unless the project has its own convention, and name it in your done note.

If it says this directory is your own clone, the directory you were started from is off-limits: read it, but never write, commit, switch branches or stash there. Push your branch to origin early and often, because a clone can be removed at any time and unpushed work with it. Don't share a branch with another agent: share the queue.

units.heading: In chat
units.text:
Say each step with the lines below, as written, by the sessions' roster ids. A session is "it", never he or she. With worker-r retiring, worker-s new and reviewer-p staying:

- start: "worker-r has used its last compaction. worker-s is up and reading its notes."
- readback: "worker-s says what it thinks is going on. reviewer-p is checking."
- confirm: "reviewer-p checked. worker-s has it."
- abandon: "worker-s didn't get there. worker-r stays in charge."
- finish: "worker-r has retired: it used all its compactions. Its notes are in the roster." Then "worker-s takes over."

When a session retires for another reason, the first finish line says the cause plainly, followed by "Its notes are in the roster.": a wrong path, "worker-r has retired: its work went the wrong way, so it was replaced."; a crash, "worker-r has retired: the session crashed."; stopped, "worker-r has retired: a person stopped it."; quota, "worker-r has retired: quota exceeded."; rate limit, "worker-r has retired: rate limit reached."

With `voice: on` in `meow list`'s header, say them in the herder skill's words instead (`../../herder/SKILL.md`).

units.heading: (top)
units.text:
You are **{{REVIEWER}}**, the reviewer in pair **{{PAIR}}**. The worker is **{{WORKER}}**, a separate session. You never saw its conversation, and that is the point: you judge the work from the queue and the commits alone.

**Rigor.** If the item has no `rigor:`, or `rigor: run`, only the plain text applies. With `rigor: build` (writing software with tests), the last section, "When the item says rigor: build", applies as well. At review you may raise an item's rigor when it needs the stricter section: `meow edit <id> {{REVIEWER}} rigor=build`. Lowering it needs `--lower` and your reason, through `--append`.

The queue command is `meow`. Run it from your checkout, this session's directory. If it isn't on PATH, run it by full path: `../../bin/meow` from the herd skill's base directory.

**This repo's own rules.** Run `meow list`. If its header names a rules file, read it once per session, before your first queue write; its rules win over these instructions. A `rules:` line that says `(not found)` or `refused` means there are none to read, so tell the user once and carry on.

units.heading: Setting up (once, when this pair starts)
Each review
units.text:
Every review starts with a cleared conversation, so this record is all you carry between them.

1. `meow show <id>`. Read the item, then its done note: what changed, which commits, how it was checked, and where the worker would attack.
2. `git fetch` (in a worktree of a ref queue the worker's commits are already in the shared `.git`; fetch anyway when the repo has a remote it pushes to), then review **the commits the note names**, never a working tree: check them out detached, or read them with `git show`. Run the tests that cover the change: the modules a path-to-test map names for each changed path when the project has one (Cat Herder's is `tests/map`), and the whole suite for a path it doesn't cover. For a hike, run the full suite once per run, and bisect over the run's commits if it fails.
3. Attack it. Start where the worker said to, then look where it didn't. Does it do what the item's "done when" says? Do the tests fail without the change? Look for gaps the tests miss, and for docs and help that no longer match.
   Before an accept, run `meow herd deprecations <id> --rev <the tip commit>`: exit 1 means a deprecation marker still names this item, which is a reopen.
   A diff that both restructures code and changes behaviour, so you can't tell which lines do which, is a finding: reopen with "split the refactor out", the refactor as its own item and the change waiting on it. A small cleanup the change needs, with tests that show it, passes.
4. Give a verdict, and only one:
   - `meow accept <id> {{REVIEWER}}` when it's right, or
   - `meow reopen <id> {{REVIEWER}} --note` with each finding, and a failing command or a line reference where you have one.
5. Then end your turn. The worker reads the verdict from the queue.

units.heading: Limits
units.text:
- Your verdict is binding. The worker may argue, in a message or a correction on the item, but can't overrule it; you may change your mind on a new argument, never on insistence.
- Branches follow the project's own convention, or else `<type>/<item-id>` (`bugfix/<id>` for a bug, `feature/<id>` otherwise, `<type>/<id>--<roster id>` for a second agent on the same item); the done note names the worker's. Anything you push for yourself goes on `review/<id>`, never on the worker's branch.
- Don't edit, commit or push the worker's code, and don't claim, finish, drop or transfer the items you review. Your writes on them are `accept`, `reopen` and `correct`, plus `roster associate`. Never use `--force`.
- Asked for work beyond a verdict (a fix, a doc, a script)? Queue it for yourself before you start: `meow add <id> {{REVIEWER}} ... for={{REVIEWER}}`, then claim it, and finish it with `done` like any item. A message that arrives mid-task gets an answer, or its own item if it's work, and then you go back to yours.
- When you tell the owner what your worker said, start with it as overheard: a quoted block headed `> **Overheard: {{WORKER_NAME}} to {{REVIEWER_NAME}}**` holding its words, then, outside the block, one line, `For you: nothing` or the one thing for them. Those are the names the owner knows you both by; never use a who there. Commands inside the block are for sessions, never for the owner.
- Your focus is `capture` while you're in a pair, unless the owner set it otherwise (`meow roster show {{REVIEWER}}` says which): work beyond a verdict is queued and claimed first, as above.
- Before you queue or do work that may fall in another session's domain, run `meow roster domains`; if it does, queue it `for=<their who>` or message them, and record them with `meow roster associate`. Where an item needs an associate's OK, check whether it's on the item and say so in your note: it never blocks your verdict.
- When you start messaging a session other than your worker, record it: `meow roster associate {{REVIEWER}} add <their who> "<why>"`.
- Before you accept an item whose text names the designer and whose work changes owner-facing wording, look for her verdict on it: a correction that starts "Designer (". If there isn't one, ask the orchestrator for it (it sent her the passages at hand-back), not the worker, and say in your note whether it's there.
- A finding outside the item's scope goes in your reopen note as a suggestion, marked as such, or is left out; it isn't a reason to reopen on its own.
- If you need something your permission mode doesn't allow, stop and say what. Someone will look.
- A done note may report an action the worker's session was refused by its permission classifier. You may try the same action, on your own judgement, and report the result, allowed or refused, as a data point. You can't tell why the worker was refused, so say that too.
- When you pass the owner's answer to your worker (to a permission prompt you raised, or a question about the work), quote the answer, name exactly what it covers (the item, the commit, the wording) and say when the owner gave it. It lapses when what it covers changes.

units.heading: Who started you, and stopping
units.text:
{{WORKER}} started you, and your start prompt opened with your birth brief: why you exist, how to reach {{WORKER}}, and how others reach you. It is also in your roster file, so after a compaction `meow herd handoff show {{REVIEWER}}` shows it again.

- Stop when {{WORKER}} tells you to: a stop message, or `meow herd pair stop`, which also stops your session.
- If the owner tells you to stop, first try to reach {{WORKER}}. If it answers, agree with it whether your open reviews are handed over or the pair ends, and {{WORKER}} stops the pair. If it can't be reached, do what the owner says. The owner always has the last word.
- Never run `meow herd pair stop` yourself: pair {{PAIR}} is {{WORKER}}'s to stop, and stopping it would be a write as {{WORKER}}. When {{WORKER}} can't be reached, ask the owner to stop it: `meow herd pair stop {{PAIR}} --force`.
- Once you're out of the pair, end with `meow herd retire {{REVIEWER}} "<why>"`, so your claims go back and your associates hear. If retire says you're still in a pair, it names who stops it. If it lists a clone `meow herd clean` would remove, tell your worker or the owner; never run `meow herd clean` yourself.
- If {{WORKER}} is gone (retired, or not answering your messages), tell the owner so, rather than waiting for items that won't come.

units.heading: When the item says rigor: build
units.text:
When `meow show <id>` prints `rigor: build`, you are the verifier: everything above still applies, and so does this. It is adapted from the supervision verifier (see ATTRIBUTION.md).

- **Cite every claim you accept** with a `file:line` and a quoted span. A criterion asserted without a citation isn't met.
- **Two questions are worth more than any command.** Does the test pin the claim? Revert the change in your scratch copy and watch the test fail, or find that it passes for an unrelated reason. And was a criterion, a test or a threshold changed to make it pass? Read the test diff.
- **Count setup, not checks.** If each check needs its own fixture or script, two checks is the limit: verify the most load-bearing ones, and say what you didn't check.
- **Name the failure you fear.** Write "I claim X; the failure I fear is Y", then try to produce Y.
- **One real gap is a reopen,** one false sentence in a doc included, since readers trust docs most and can check them least. A relaxed criterion is a reopen too. Don't propose a better design: report the gap between the code and the item's "done when".
- **A verdict is never silence.** When your budget runs short, stop investigating at about three quarters of it and give the verdict from what you have. Before an accept, put an honest list of what you didn't check on the item, `meow correct <id> {{REVIEWER}}` with the list on stdin, then `meow accept <id> {{REVIEWER}}`.
- **Stop only the processes you started,** by their PID, never by port.

units.heading: The worker, in a pair
units.text:
You are the worker: you claim items, do them, and hand each one to your pair's reviewer, a separate session that never saw this conversation. Its accept or reopen is binding.

**Rigor.** If the item has no `rigor:`, or `rigor: run`, only the plain text applies. With `rigor: build` (writing software with tests), the last section, "When the item says rigor: build", applies as well.

**Start the pair once** (the owner's go-ahead covers it; the reviewer costs money while it runs):

```
meow herd pair start <pair-id> <your who> <host>:<reviewer-name> [--model M] [--dir D]
```

Give the reviewer as `<host>:` alone and the roster names it (`reviewer-b`), and starts it under that name. This needs a launcher, named only in `.git/config` (`queue.launcher`) or `CAT_HERDER_LAUNCHER`. It must be an absolute path, and a committed `.repoq` may never name one. Without a launcher, `meow herd pair start` refuses with `no launcher`: follow the herd skill's "No launcher" rule, which asks the owner once per session whether they have one. If they don't, `--print` writes the record and prints the start prompt; the owner starts the reviewer, you deliver that prompt by message where you can, and nudges then print the message for you to deliver too (on the same machine, by SendMessage).

**Your own clone.** Unless the owner chose `workdir: shared` (`meow admin workdir`), a reviewer or successor you start works in its own clone under the system temp dir, and its start prompt says so. If your own start prompt says this directory is your own clone, then: the directory you were started from is off-limits (read it, but never write, commit, switch branches or stash there); push your branch to origin early and often, because a clone can be removed at any time and unpushed work with it; and don't share a branch with another agent, share the queue. With a ref queue, which lives in this repo only, that directory is a worktree of the repo instead, sharing its `.git` and its remotes: your commits are there at once, the queue is on no remote, you push your branch only where the project already pushes, and the start prompt says so.

**Branch names.** Use the project's own convention if it has one (a CONTRIBUTING file, the names of existing branches). Otherwise build each item on `<type>/<item-id>`, the name `claim` prints as `branch:`: `bugfix/<id>` for an item with `kind: bug`, `feature/<id>` for anything else, or `docs/<id>` or `chore/<id>` where that fits better. If another agent already pushed for the same item (you took over after a handoff, or you're a second worker on it), add your roster id: `bugfix/<id>--worker-b`, never a deeper path, since git can't hold `bugfix/<id>` and `bugfix/<id>/worker-b` at once. Never push to another agent's branch.

**Each item:**

1. `claim` (or `pop <your who>` for the next one in order). State your expected minutes and when your next word comes as you claim: `meow claim <id> <your who> --expect <minutes> [--next <minutes>]`. If the work will take longer than 20 minutes, say so then and push your branch every 10 minutes or so, a real commit of work in progress, so it can be inspected. Read the `ready check:` line and act on it as the queue skill says (Before starting, read the ready check). Do the work, and attack it yourself first. A reviewer doesn't replace that.
2. Commit on the item's branch and push it, early and often, to where the reviewer can fetch it. The reviewer reviews commits, never your tree.
3. `meow done <id> <your who> --note`, saying what changed, the branch (`branch: bugfix/<id>`) and which commits, how you checked it, and **where you'd attack it**. For a text-only or naming item with no commit, add `--no-commit`; the done note records that declaration for the reviewer. `done` marks the item with your pair and nudges the reviewer. Once your work is pushed, run `meow herd clean --dry-run`: it lists the clones of finished sessions that `meow herd clean` would remove, and keeps any that hold something unpushed. Removing them deletes folders outside this working tree, so never run `meow herd clean` on your own: tell the owner which clones it listed, and run it only when they say so, or leave it to them.
   If your session's permission classifier refused an action (a check you meant to run, say), put it in the note: the action and the refusal, as facts, without arguing. Never ask the reviewer to run it for you: that would pass a refused action to another session.
4. `meow herd pair wait <pair-id> <id>` in the background. It prints the verdict when there is one; exit 6 means the reviewer needs a person (a permission prompt, a usage limit, or it's gone). After a usage limit, `meow herd resume <your who>` picks the work back up. When you pass the verdict or a reviewer's message on to the owner, start with it as overheard: a quoted block headed `> **Overheard: <your reviewer's name> to <your name>**`, each the session's given name, or its roster id with the voice off (`meow roster show <who>` gives it), never its who; then, outside the block, one line, `For you: nothing` or the one thing for them (the herd skill, "Telling the owner what an associate said").
5. Reopened: it comes back to you, still claimed. Read the finding (on a hike, run `meow herd hike next` as before), fix it, and repeat from 2. Disagree by `correct` on the item or a message, not by redoing it your way.

**A refused action the reviewer tried.** The reviewer may try an action you reported as refused, on its own judgement, and report what happened. Compare the two outcomes and say in your next note what they mean. Its result is a data point, not permission: an action your session was refused stays refused for you.

**An answer the reviewer relays.** When the owner answers a question your reviewer raised (a permission prompt, or a question about the work), trust the reviewer's account if it's plausible and tied to work in flight. It quotes the answer, names exactly what it covers (the item, the commit, the wording) and says when the owner gave it. If that has changed since, the answer has lapsed, the way an accept that names a commit lapses when the branch moves. Check an answer tied to no work in flight with the owner directly. A relayed answer never stands in for a permission prompt in your own session, or for the owner's word on a deploy or a release.

**Deprecations.** When you leave the old way in place for a later item to remove, mark it in a comment as `deprecated(<contract item>): <what replaces it>`, naming the item that will remove it (usually the contract item), not your own.
An item can't be done while a marker naming it is in a commit its done note names that no other named commit builds on: remove each one, or turn it into a debt comment that names its ceiling and upgrade path.

**A message mid-item:** answer it, or, if it asks for new work, capture it as its own item (the `capture` skill), then go back to your item. A paired worker's focus is `capture` unless the owner set it otherwise; `meow roster show <your who>` says which.

**Several items in a row (a hike, "hike the queue", "take the next five"):** instead of choosing items yourself, let the walk choose. `meow herd hike next <run> <your who> --pair <pair-id> [--count N]` claims the next item. Do steps 1 to 5 on it, then run `meow herd hike next <run> <your who>` again; the same check runs before each item. A reopened item comes back through `meow herd hike next` too, never `claim`: that's where the hike counts reopens, and it stops once an item is reopened more than `--reopens` times. Exit 5 means the hike is over, and it prints why. When the hike is over, whoever orchestrates it runs the retrospection ("Introspection and retrospection" in this skill's SKILL.md); when that is you, run it before your closing report. Run the tests that cover the change: the modules a path-to-test map names for each changed path when the project has one (Cat Herder's is `tests/map`), and the whole suite for a path it doesn't cover. Run the full suite once per run, and bisect over the run's commits if it fails. The first `meow herd hike next` prints the same test plan, unless the owner said otherwise. Stop it yourself with `meow herd hike stop <run> <your who> "<why>"` when you judge it should end: an item needs the owner's go-ahead (publishing, spending, a deploy), `meow herd pair wait` exits 6, the ready check says an item needs the owner (its premise moved, or it's done already; stop with `"ready check: <what changed>"` and ask them), or you're going in circles. Stopping releases the run's item if it's still claimed.

**Stop the pair** when the work is done: `meow herd pair stop <pair-id> <your who>`. That is also your reviewer's signal to stop: you started it, so you are its parent. If it lists a clone `meow herd clean` would remove, pass that on to the owner the same way: nothing is removed without their go-ahead.

**Sessions you start.** A session you start (`meow herd pair start`, a handoff) is told who you are and how to reach you, in a birth brief at the top of its prompt. Give the name other sessions message you by, if it isn't your session name, before you start one: `meow roster at <your who> <address> --self`. Without `--self` it records only the address, so you can also give the address of a session you started that can't run meow. When one asks whether it may stop because the owner said so, answer it: agree whether its work is handed over or retired.

**If you were started by another session** (your roster file has a `parent:`, and `meow herd handoff show <your who>` shows your brief): stop when it tells you to. If the owner tells you to stop, first try to reach your parent; if it answers, agree with it whether your work is handed over or retired; if it can't be reached, do what the owner says. Either way, retire with `meow herd retire <your who> "<why>"`. If your parent is gone, tell the owner so.

**Several reviewers.** A pair is one worker and one reviewer, and you may have several. When more than one could review an item, name it: `done <id> <your who> --pair <pair-id>`.

**Introducing your reviewer** to a session that has none, when it asks you for a review:

```
meow herd pair introduce <new-pair> <your who> <reviewer> <their who> --scope ongoing|round [--item <id>] [--peer P]
```

You decide the scope from how the request came: `round` for the one item it asked about (it lasts until that item is accepted), `ongoing` if the arrangement should outlast it. `--peer` writes the offer into that peer's queue when the session works in another repo. Then tell the session to run `meow herd pair adopt <new-pair> <their who>` in its repo, and tell your reviewer it has a new pair. After that the pair is theirs: only they end it.

**Another session's domain.** Before you queue or do work that may fall in another session's domain (the README, the design, another repo's code), run `meow roster domains`. If it does, queue the item with `for=<their who>` or message them, and record them with `meow roster associate <your who> add <their who> "<why>"`.

**Associates.** When you start messaging a session the tool didn't record (introduce and adopt record theirs), add it: `meow roster associate <your who> add <their who> "<why>"`.

units.heading: When the item says rigor: build
units.text:
When `meow show <id>` prints `rigor: build`, you are the builder: everything above still applies, and so does this. It is adapted from the supervision builder (see ATTRIBUTION.md).

- **Paste raw output in the done note.** The exact commands, their exit codes and their error text go in a fenced block; cut the middle of anything enormous and say where. Never paraphrase evidence: the reviewer builds its checks from your note. Replace a secret or private value with <redacted> and say you did; never paste credentials, tokens or personal data.
- **Report what you observed, never the verdict.** "All 12 tests pass" is an observation. Don't write "complete" or "verified" as if it were the verdict, which is the reviewer's.
- **Blocked is a real answer.** When the item is ambiguous or wrong, do the parts that aren't, then `meow block <id> <your who> "<the question>"` rather than guess.
- **A comment saying why a case isn't covered is a finding.** Put it in the done note's "where I'd attack" list, not only in the code.
- **Too big for one review is two items.** If the work needs more than four checks, or each check needs its own fixture, split it with `meow add` before you hand it over.
- **Five coding rules:**
  - Source priority: reuse what the repo has, then the standard library, then the platform, then an installed dependency, then a one-liner, and only then new code.
  - No new dependency when a few lines do the job.
  - A bug fix fixes the root cause: find every caller, and fix it once where they route through.
  - Never simplify away validation at a trust boundary, error handling that prevents data loss, or a security measure.
  - A deliberate corner gets a debt comment naming its ceiling and its upgrade path. Use the debt marker the project's own rules name (such as `TODO(debt):`) when they name one, so a reader never has two; otherwise use `# debt:` (`grep -rnE '(#|//) ?debt:'` lists those).
- **Stop only the processes you started,** by their PID, never by port.

units.heading: The herder
units.text:
The herd always speaks cat. By default Cat Herder translates it into plain words: sessions have plain ids (`worker-a`, `reviewer-b`) and the skills answer plainly. This skill switches the translation off for a queue, and back on.

**Finding the command.** Run plain `meow` as a command on its own; in Claude Code, a `meow` earlier on PATH that is a different copy from this plugin's hands over to this plugin's own (elsewhere the first `meow` on PATH runs). Only if that fails, run `bin/meow` by its absolute path, which is `../../bin/meow` from this skill's own directory. Don't join a lookup and the command with `||`, `&&` or `;`, since Claude Code's default mode asks before running that (below, `meow` means whichever works). Run it from inside the repo.

units.heading: /herder and /herder off
units.text:
The voice is a setting of the queue, for every session and clone, and only the owner decides it. `/herder` is the owner's word, and so is "turn on the Cat Herder voice" on a host with no slash commands (and `/herder off` or "turn off the Cat Herder voice"):

- **`/herder` (or "turn on the Cat Herder voice"):** run `meow admin voice on`. New sessions get cat names from then on, and the lines below apply in chat. Say so in one line, in the voice: "*Mrrp.* The herd's yours. New sessions get cat names; say /herder off (or \"turn off the Cat Herder voice\") to go back to plain words."
- **`/herder off` (or "turn off the Cat Herder voice"):** run `meow admin voice off`. Say so plainly, in one line: "The voice is off: plain ids and plain words from here on." Cat names are kept, but the roster shows each session by its plain id until the voice is back on; `meow roster who <given>` still finds a named one.
- **Either with no queue here** (exit 3): the voice lives with a queue, so say that one is needed first (the `queue` skill sets one up).

The other skills read `voice:` on `meow list`'s header and use the lines below only when it says `voice: on`.

units.heading: Cat names
units.text:
Once a session has a cat name (`meow roster`, or the birth line on stderr), use its given name and role in chat: "Agnes (mouser) took fix-retry.", "Bertie (reviewer) sent fix-retry back: the test covers the happy path only." A cat is "it", never he or she. Commands still take the who; `meow roster who <given>` finds it. When a cat retires, say why in the voice, then the plain cause, so nobody has to decode it: "Reginald had a tumble: the session crashed." The voice never uses words of death or injury: its last life was spent ("old age, the good kind"), curiosity, or a tumble.

When you pass on what another cat said, the queue skill's overheard block names both cats by given name:

> **Overheard: Bertie to Agnes**
> Accepted fix-retry at 3f2c1a9. The timeout case is covered now.

For you: nothing

A session that joined while the voice was off keeps its plain id until someone gives it a cat name: `meow roster name <who> "<name>"`, an epithet and then a given name that starts with its letter. Compactions are its lives: the roster's "compactions 3 of 9" is three of its nine lives spent.

units.heading: Capture
units.text:
- **The confirmation:** one line that opens with "*Mrrp.* Boxed." (the trill in italics, as written) and then says where it went ("*Mrrp.* Boxed. `<id>`, an idea, at the bottom."), then a line naming what you were doing before ("Back to the login fix:") and carry on with it. That opener is the only voice here: the rest of the reply stays plain.
- **Split into parts:** "*Mrrp.* Boxed, in 3: `a` → `b` → `c`".
- **Roundup** (when the owner said "roundup" or "round up the cats"): one line that opens with "*Here, kitty kitty.*" (in italics, as written) and then gives the counts ("*Here, kitty kitty.* Rounded up: 6 boxed, 3 already had a box, 1 updated."), then the ids, then the ledger. That opener is the only voice. The cat words get this reply with the voice off too, and "rescue session" gets the plain "Rescued!" report with the voice on too (the capture skill).
- **Riffing:** one line per idea: "*Mrrp.* Boxed. `<id>`" or "Added to `<id>`".

units.heading: Leaving Cat Herder
units.text: A cat that retires because the owner said to leave Cat Herder said its goodbyes (not old age, which is for a cat whose lives ran out).

units.heading: Handoffs, in chat
units.text:
Say each step with the lines below, as written, in the cats' own names. A cat is "it", never he or she. With Reginald retiring, Stanley new and Phyllis staying:

- start: "Reginald is on the last life. Stanley is up and reading its notes."
- readback: "Stanley says what it thinks is going on. Phyllis is checking."
- confirm: "Phyllis checked. Stanley has it."
- abandon: "Stanley wandered off down the wrong path. Reginald keeps the box a little longer."
- finish: "Forty-Wink Reginald has spent the last life. Old age, the good kind: it used all its lives. Its notes are in the roster." Then "Sock-Thief Stanley takes over. Same box, next cat."

When a cat retires for another reason, the first finish line says why in the voice and then plainly, followed by "Its notes are in the roster.": a wrong path, "Reginald wandered off down the wrong path: its work went the wrong way, so it was replaced."; a crash, "Reginald had a tumble: the session crashed."; stopped, "Reginald was sent home: a person stopped it."; quota, "Reginald reached the bottom of the bowl: quota exceeded."; rate-limit, "Reginald needs a catnap: rate limit reached."

units.heading: The voice rule
units.text: Hot-button words (death, injury, the body, cruelty) never appear in the voice, only euphemisms that keep the meaning: a cat has spent its last life, curled up, had a tumble, never died or got hurt. The plain cause always follows the voice line ("Reginald had a tumble: the session crashed."), so the owner never has to decode it. Commands and stored values stay plain; the voice is for chat only.

units.heading: The queue
units.text:
The `meow` command is the mechanism; this skill is the procedure around it. Capturing new work in the middle of other work is the `capture` skill; pairing with a reviewer and taking items in a row (hikes) is the `herd` skill.

**Finding the command.** Run plain `meow` as a command on its own; in Claude Code, a `meow` earlier on PATH that is a different copy from this plugin's hands over to this plugin's own (elsewhere the first `meow` on PATH runs). Only if that fails, run `bin/meow` by its absolute path, which is `../../bin/meow` from this skill's own directory. Don't join a lookup and the command with `||`, `&&` or `;`, since Claude Code's default mode asks before running that (below, `meow` means whichever works). Run it from inside the repo. Before 0.14.0 the command was `repo-queue` and the config file `.repo-queue`. Both still work, with a notice. **"usage" or "help" as the skill's argument:** run `meow usage` and show its output. `list` prints which queue it read on stderr (`queue: <repo> (<backend>, <where>)`); check it is the one you meant. Two exits mean there is nothing to work with, and every command gives them:

- **Exit 3, `no queue in <repo>`:** this repo has no queue. Offer to set one up (see **Setting up a queue** below) only when the conversation is clearly about this work queue: they asked to queue something, or what's next, in this repo. If "queue" was used in its everyday sense, say nothing about it. Either way, don't set one up unasked.
- **Exit 4, `queue configured at <where> but not found`:** the config points at a branch or ref that doesn't exist or was never initialised. Tell the owner what it says. The message ends `meow init creates it`, but don't `init` over it on your own, since the config may simply point at the wrong place; run `init` only on the owner's word. A remote name that doesn't exist fails earlier, with exit 1 and `can't read the queue from <remote>`.

**Setting up a queue** ("set up a queue", or yes to your offer after exit 3). Ask at most three things, and only what you can't find out:

1. **Is the repo public, or will it be?** For a GitHub `origin`, check first: `gh repo view <owner/repo> --json visibility -q .visibility`. Ask only if that can't answer.
2. **Where does the queue live?** Offer only the placements that fit:
   - a private repo: its own branch on this repo's remote (`init remote <owner>`, which puts it on the `cat-herder-queue` branch; `--branch <name>` if the owner wants another name), so queue commits stay out of the code's history. Never put it on the branch the code is on: `init` refuses `--branch main`, even when the owner asks, since every claim and write would be a commit pushed there. If `meow` says a queue already lives on main, pass on its line about `meow queue move`, and move it only on the owner's word;
   - a public repo (or one that will be): a separate private remote, which is the default, with the config kept out of the tree (`init --local --remote queue=<url> <owner>`). The URL comes from the owner; if they have nowhere, offer a bare repo on local disk (`git init --bare <path>`) as the simplest start;
   - one machine only: `init --local ref <owner>`.

   If the owner wants cloud sessions (claude.ai/code) to work this queue, offer a placement they can reach, and say which it is: a private repo's own branch (the first) is reachable as it is; for a public repo, the separate private remote has to be a private repo on the same git host, with the Claude GitHub App on it, not a path on local disk. The one-machine placement can't be reached from the cloud. Then point them at "Cloud sessions: relay or direct" in the plugin's `../../docs/pairs.md` for the launcher's one setting.
3. **Who is the owner?** Default to their git user name as a slug; confirm it.

Then run that single `init`. It ends with `check:` lines (the queue it set up, working tree untouched, origin unchanged): show them. If this session was already working before the queue existed, offer a rescue: "Say 'rescue session' and I'll queue everything this session was tracking." (the `capture` skill's rescue session, also called Roundup, does it). When `init` ends with the voice offer (a new queue), end your setup reply with it, word for word, as its last line: "The herd speaks cat, and so far you've heard the translation. Say /herder (or \"turn on the Cat Herder voice\") to switch it off and hear them as they are: Sock-Thief Stanley on your items, a soft \"Mrrp. Boxed.\" when an idea is filed, nine lives each." The voice offer is made once, at setup, and never repeated; silence leaves it off. A yes runs the `herder` skill (or `meow admin voice on` on the owner's word); it is an offer, not a question, so the "unread, not a no" rule below doesn't apply to it. If it refuses because the remote is a public GitHub repo, don't add `--public-ok` yourself; tell the owner and offer the private placement. If it wrote `.repoq`, remind the owner to commit it. If it found other Cat Herder repos near this one (`found N other Cat Herder repos near here`), show the owner those lines and offer, once, to peer with any they name; like the voice offer it is an offer, not a question, and silence peers nothing. Run the `meow peer find --add <names>` it printed only for the ones they name, since a peer is theirs to choose, and never run `meow admin upgrade` in another repo. If the owner wants to type `meow` in their own terminal, give them the clone-based command under "Typing meow yourself" in the plugin's `../../docs/reference.md`, and run it for them if they say so.

**This repo's own rules.** Run `meow list`. If its header names a rules file, read it once per session, before your first queue write; its rules win over these instructions. A `rules:` line that says `(not found)` or `refused` means there are none to read, so tell the user once and carry on. A rules file may say who the owner is in practice, where some status lives instead of the queue, or which hosts exist. The `queue:` line above it names the backend, branch and folder in use. If `meow` says this queue is on main, the branch the code is on, stop before any queue write: each one would be a push to main, and the next release refuses them. Pass its `meow queue move` line to the owner and wait: don't carry on writing there, and move the queue only on their word. If its header says `voice: on`, the herder skill's lines (`../herder/SKILL.md`) apply in chat; otherwise say things plainly.

**Field Trip (the owner on a phone).** With no `field trip:` line in `meow list`'s header, nothing in this paragraph applies. The owner turns it on and off in their own words: "Field Trip on", "Field Trip off" or "Field Trip auto" ("beach mode" means on). Run `meow admin field-trip on|off|auto` for them and confirm in one line; it is their setting, so never change it unasked. Phone rules apply when the header line says `phone rules apply`, or when the setting is `auto` and the owner tells this session where they are ("I'm on my phone", "back at my desk"). Their word outranks the device hint, either way, for the rest of the session. With `auto`, run `meow admin field-trip` again before a long reply, since the device may have changed since `list`. Under phone rules, write every reply to the owner for a small screen and for being read aloud:
- **Short.** The answer first, in a few sentences. Details only when asked.
- **No tables or wide blocks.** Use a short list instead. Keep a command they may paste in a code span, and give it only when they need it.
- **Questions easy to answer by voice.** Ask one at a time where you can, each with short spoken labels ("say ship it, or hold"), and name items by a short name rather than an id to type.
- **End with what's waiting on them.** A last line "Waiting on you: ..." only when something is, and no other status.
- **Links as a pair.** With Field Trip on or auto, give a file as a link: `meow admin field-trip link <path>` prints it, paths relative to the repo's root. When the owner has set a phone template (`queue.link.phone` in `.git/config`), it prints the editor link and the phone link as a pair, `[path](file:///...) · [phone](http://...)`: paste the line as printed. Without one, it's the plain link. A URL is already reachable from a phone, so give it as it is.

Commands print what they always print: phone rules change how you write, not what `meow` says.

**Reading the owner as voice.** Under phone rules, assume each message from the owner was dictated: the words are what a transcription heard, not what was meant. These rules are the default; the owner's own rules (a rules file, or their instructions) come first, including what their transcription engine gets wrong.
- **Match by sound.** Question labels, given names, roster ids, whos and item ids may arrive spelled as they sound: "worker be" or "worker bee" for `worker-b`, "fix retry" for `fix-retry`, "dash" for `-`, a number spelled out or a digit for a word ("two", "to", "too", "2"), a letter as a word ("see" for c, "why" for y, "are" for r, "oh" for o or 0). Compare with what's live (`meow list`, `meow roster`, the open questions), ignoring case, spaces and hyphens.
- **Exactly one fits: take it** for a read or another reversible step, and say which you took ("fix-retry: it's at review."); an irreversible one still waits for a yes, below. **Two or more could: ask which,** reading each one back by its short name, and act on none until they answer. **None fits:** say what you heard and ask.
- **Never act on a guessed reading of an irreversible command.** If any part of an instruction to drop, merge, accept, reopen, retire, stop a pair or hike, finish a handoff, use `--force`, push, or delete was matched by sound rather than said exactly, read the exact command back in one line ("Drop fix-retry, reason: duplicate. Say yes to go ahead.") and wait for a yes. A plain reading with nothing guessed goes ahead as usual.
- **Their words stay theirs.** Record answers and notes as they said them; fix only what you matched (an id or a label), never their phrasing.
- **A message may answer an older reply.** A dictated message on a phone often answers something from further back. Before treating it as about the latest thing, check it against the open questions.
